chapter: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
title: Rex Stewart: cornet, third trumpet, and selling a sour note
summary: Rex Stewart was an aggressive ear player on third trumpet who could sell a blue note to a packed house, as at the Graystone battle; he pumped his stomach and drew laughs.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: But just let your mind flit back to those people and those times, and we'll go from there. We have talked about Rex Stewart, of course, several times here, and I'm not sure if there's more that we can say, but I'll just bring his name up.
Well, you're going to talk about some real characters in some of these fellows, --
Great.

-- but actually it was a great experience for me because they all had different personalities; yet they were great musicians, and, of course, starting out with Rex Stewart, I was fortunate enough to have Rex Stewart in my band with the Wilberforce Collegiates, along with Benny Carter.
Right.

And Rex was playing the cornet at that time, and he was always an aggressive sort of fellow. He wasn't one of the greatest sort of what you call sight readers in the world, but he had quite an ear, and, of course, in my band as well as in Fletcher's band he more or less played third trumpet, you know, and, of course, as you know, not playing the lead, you can skate a little bit if you've got a good ear, you know, what I mean by like-skate.
And, of course, on the solos he was terrific, and he was one of the few trumpet players --
(Inaudible portion) INSERT
So this was what the people ate up.
Did he hit those notes intentionally?
No. No. No.
He'd just miss them.
INSERT TO p. 3

... that I ever had the pleasure of working with or hearing, for that matter, that could make a sour note, which we call a blure, and sell it, and it would sound good. Not on the recordings, of course, but when we would play to a packed house, like in the Graystone Ballroom in Detroit, Michigan, for instance. I know we had a battle of music there, the Wilberforce Collegians and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, which was quite a band in those days. And we had a battle of music out in the garden where had had about five or six thousand people. And Rex could sell, and he would play this little cornet. And he looked real funny, because he was a hefty guy anyway, and playing the little horn, it looked like he was taking advantage of that horn. And he would scream on a note, and it probably had the original intention of being a C, and he made it a C sharp or out of key deal that had no relation to the chord at all. But he sold it.

It was he just -- the force that he put behind his horn and he didn't have the correct schooling like most first trumpet players, you know, so I mean he had to make it up by being a salesman, and when he would play, he would do something in music in what we call -- rather -- he would pump, see, you know. It was funny to watch, you know, and the people loved that. They didn't even pay attention to what he was playing, what was coming out of the horn. They were looking at the individual, you know.
I see. He was moving his body and --
Oh, he was funny. You could see his stomach moving in and out. He -- why he drew laughs and everything and applause too, you know. So this was Rex Stewart.
As the leader, did it bother you, like in the beginning when he was hitting these clinker notes, or did, you know, it immediately appeal to you, or how did you feel about that?

Well, I tell you, there weren't that many clinkers that he hit. Just when he would snatch for high notes, you know, reach for the high notes, we call it. But he had an uncanny ear, and you played something down once, an arrangement, he's got his part. He might even put in a few weird notes that weren't on the paper, for harmony, you know? And as long as it would sound pleasing to him, one of those
things, or pleasing to me, I would, you know, accept it. But he was a salesman and he was a hard worker at all times. Now this all happened in my band.
Right.
